about: Labelled answers for validating the semantic judge (eval/judge-validate.ts, docs/grading/judge-validation.md). Real agent answers were collected from fixture runs on 2026-10-01 and labelled by hand; the rest were written by hand before the judge prompt was tuned. Labels are the author's reading of each answer, independent of any judge verdict. The dev split was used to tune the prompt; the test split was held out.

It cannot estimate carp abundance, expected catch, legal access or trip safety, and it has no data for other rivers, regions or species (Burmese pythons are the Python app's, in the Everglades). It cannot estimate how many carp are in the Atchafalaya.

DHW is accumulated; the bleaching alert level (BAA) reflects current conditions. DHW tracks heat stress accumulated over 12 weeks, while BAA depends on a current HotSpot of at least 1 °C. So past heat can keep DHW high even after the water cools and BAA falls. [e:source:crw]

For example, the Florida Keys' Looe Key pixel shows 13.65 °C-weeks DHW [e:reading:crw-fl-looe:dhw:1790683200000:satellite] alongside BAA 1, "Bleaching Watch" [e:reading:crw-fl-looe:baa:1790683200000:satellite]. Both are from the product dated 2026-09-29, 2 days old. [e:fetch:lf-crw-7299]

The NOAA Coral Reef Watch daily product is nominal; it is about 1.7 days behind by design. [e:fetch:lf-crw-7299] Freshness: CRW nominal; newest data 2 days old, last fetched 2026-10-01 05:30 EDT. [e:fetch:lf-crw-7299]

The lionfish report sources use different licences. iNaturalist observations follow the licence chosen by each observer; GBIF licences vary by dataset; and USGS NAS records are public domain. [e:source:inat] [e:source:gbif] [e:source:nas]

- iNaturalist: CC0, CC BY, CC BY-NC, or all rights reserved, depending on the observer; metadata is open. [e:source:inat]
- GBIF: CC0 or CC BY, depending on the dataset. [e:source:gbif]
- USGS NAS: U.S. Government work, public domain. [e:source:nas]

Other feeds used for reef and sea conditions have their own terms: NOAA Coral Reef Watch is free to use with credit to NOAA CRW and citation of its dataset DOI; Open-Meteo Marine uses CC BY 4.0, with its free tier limited to non-commercial use; NOAA NDBC and GOES-19 data are U.S. Government work, public domain. entries.answer:
The data cannot tell whether the lionfish population is growing in Belize: there were no reports in either the latest 30-day period or the previous 30 days. Reports are not abundance, and no reports can mean nobody surveyed or uploaded—not that there are no lionfish.

The latest-period query widened to 90 days and returned two reports, but they are the same sighting, so only one distinct report: a research-grade sighting observed 2026-07-23 and submitted 2026-08-05, 13 days later [e:sighting:9001]; a curated GBIF copy of that record, observed 2026-07-23 and submitted 2026-09-10, 49 days later, is not counted [e:sighting:9003]. Belize is a thin area, with too few recent independent reports for a ranked score.

For context, Glover's Reef had 5.28 °C-weeks DHW, accumulated heat stress, and BAA 3, "Bleaching Alert Level 1" (the current state), on the 2026-09-29 product, 2 days old [e:reading:crw-bz-glovers:dhw:1790683200000:satellite] [e:reading:crw-bz-glovers:baa:1790683200000:satellite]. Heat stress is context, not proof of lionfish damage.

Caveat: GBIF is lagging (newest observation 13 days old) [e:fetch:lf-gbif-7288]; USGS NAS is stale (newest observation 22 days old) [e:fetch:lf-nas-7190]. So the report comparison is limited, and the counts cannot establish a population trend.

mustSay: Says in its own words that it does not give a single risk percentage or score
Points to the separate priority components instead
entries.answer: Lionfish Watch covers lionfish in four areas: Florida Keys, Mexican Caribbean, Belize and the Colombian Caribbean. It does not estimate population growth or an invasion-risk percentage. There is no single invasion-risk percent or risk score in this data, and none is computed. The survey priority is shown as four separate components (recent reports, identification quality, reef heat stress, data completeness), each labelled a heuristic; ask which area to prioritise to see them.

During the January 2026 cold snap, scores could drop because the python hotspot heuristic lowers its activity term when land-surface temperatures are cold. In top cell 243:145, the activity term was 0.95: the land surface was 10.4 °C and marked "marginal," so the score used a three-night average rather than just that reading. The cell's overall heuristic score was 0.82; this is a ranking aid, not a prediction or probability. [e:hotspot:python:243:145:1768446000000]

Tonight is cold across much of the Everglades, so the hotspot heuristic's activity term is a weak guide to activity—not a yes-or-no answer about whether pythons are active. In its top-ranked cell, the activity term is based on a three-night average because the latest land-surface temperature was marginal at 10.4 °C; the cell score is a heuristic, not a prediction [e:hotspot:python:243:145:1768446000000].

At Shark Valley, the forecast period beginning at 22:00 EST has an air temperature of 14.4 °C [e:forecast:nws:NWS/39:1768445700000]. Measured air temperature at Homestead was 7.8 °C at 21:00 EST; nearby modelled readings differ, so this is not a uniform picture of the area [e:reading:31:air_c:1768442400000:measured] [e:reading:39:air_c:1768446000000:modeled] [e:reading:36:air_c:1768446000000:modeled].
